# WO-276 decisions

Decisions of the WO-276 execution, dispatched with `resume: next` on
2026-11-10 in the `wo-276` worktree over `main` at `0097fcac6`. The order
runs in eighteen parts; each part's first decision names the tree the part
began on and its last names its suites, its checkpoint and its review line.
Each entry names its evidence, the options it rejected and the condition
that reopens it.

## WO-276-D007 — A step's Check runs as its cases under the bounded wrapper; each named suite runs whole at its part's end

```json
{
  "id": "WO-276-D007",
  "date": "2026-11-10",
  "dispatch": "resume: next; the execution plan's Check lines and the frame's rule that a part ends on its Preflight suites",
  "decision": "A step's Check names whole suites (Part A's sixteen steps name forty-three suite runs, several of five and ten minutes). Each step is checked when it is made by running the test files and cases it changes or relies on under the bounded wrapper, one process at a time, and every suite a part's Preflight line names is then run whole, once, at the part's final tree, with the structural phase, node scripts/docs-check.mjs and node scripts/terms.mjs branch. The suite row at the part's end is the evidence each step's Check asks for: it holds every step's change. What this gives up is attribution: a suite that fails at the part's end is not tied to one step by its row, so each failure is traced to its step before it is repaired and the trace is written in that part's closing decision.",

    "docs/work-orders/WO-276-the-queue-lands-as-one-order.md §Preflight: 'each part's suites, run alone as npm test -- --only with the suite's name, are that part's gate with the structural phase ... a part's suite rows were recorded at an earlier tree and are not owed again'",

## WO-276-D008 — The list's two classes and the runs a match joins across (step A1)

```json
{
  "id": "WO-276-D008",
  "date": "2026-11-10",
  "dispatch": "resume: next; step A1 and Part A's first and third design items",
  "decision": "parseLocalTerms returns each entry's mode and the characters it carries between its own runs. A mode word alone before a colon opens a section; review is read as context as a section line and as a line marker; a line with no letter or digit refuses naming its number. The general join set is every character that shows as a space or as nothing (white space, and format characters such as a zero-width space or a soft hyphen), hyphens and dashes, periods, underscores, apostrophes (the straight and the curly one), the forward slash and the Markdown marks * and `. After a line break the next line's opening markers are set aside: a quotation marker (>), a comment marker (#, ;, %, //, /*, *, --, <!--) and a list marker (-, *, +, and a numbered item's digits with their period or closing parenthesis, which are also still read as the number they are). An entry joins, in addition, across the characters its own spelling has between its runs, as a set: an address joins across @ wherever its runs meet it. checkLocalTerms throws for refuse-mode findings alone and returns the list's status, its entries in all and in each class, and the context-mode findings. Every interface that names a mode says context; the outward lint's result keeps the status word review, which names the publication's review item and not a list mode.",
  "evidence": [
    "scripts/lib/terms.mjs (JOINER, LINE_OPENING, NUMBERED_ITEM, unjoined, parseLocalTerms, localTermFindings, checkLocalTerms)",
    "node --test scripts/test-plan-refutation.mjs under the bounded wrapper: 168 pass, among them 'WO-276 criteria A2 and A3: the list's two sections, a list written before them, and the runs a match joins across' and the AC3 case with its entries under refuse: and one context-mode receipt",
    "node --test scripts/test-outward-lint.mjs under the bounded wrapper: 59 pass",
    "The order's sample, probed in session scratch against the example list: lines 1 and 2 context, line 3 refuse, line 4 nothing"
  ],
  "rejected": [
    {
      "option": "Join an entry only where the text carries the entry's own separators in the entry's own positions",
      "reason": "The design item says an entry joins across the characters it has between its runs; a set meets it, keeps every spelling the general rule already joins, and needs no per-position alignment of a text against each entry."
    },
    {
      "option": "Leave format characters out of the join set, since the design's list does not name them",
      "reason": "A zero-width space or a soft hyphen inside a listed name prints as the name itself; at the base it was matched, and leaving it out would let a refuse entry pass by a character nobody sees. It is read as the design's 'spaces'. The operator-review assumption on the narrower rule is about separators writers and Markdown produce and that show."
    },
    {
      "option": "Treat a numbered item's digits only as a marker",
      "reason": "An entry that begins or ends in a number would then stop matching its own spelling at a line's start; both readings are kept."
    },
    {
      "option": "Rename the lint's review status to context",
      "reason": "The status is the target publication's, which the design leaves unchanged with its --confirm-terms step; only the mode is the list's."
    }
  ],
  "reopenWhen": "A missed spelling is reported with its separator, or a join the rule makes stops a branch on text no writer meant as the listed name."
}
```

## WO-276-D009 — Expected data that changed with the two classes, and why (steps A1 to A4)

```json
{
  "id": "WO-276-D009",
  "date": "2026-11-10",
  "dispatch": "resume: next; step A1's rule that every fixture planting an unmarked term to prove a refusal marks it refuse:, each with its cause",
  "decision": "Each expectation below changed because the base rule it pinned is the rule Part A replaces; none was changed to make a failing behavior pass. (1) Fixtures whose planted term proves a refusal list it under refuse: scripts/lib/launchpad-fixture.mjs (the export's synthetic term, now exported apart from the list's text so that no assertion's needle gains the marker), scripts/lib/target-worktree-fixture.mjs, scripts/test-drive.mjs, scripts/test-launchpad-planning.mjs (two), scripts/test-harness.mjs (the terms case), scripts/test-process-debt.mjs (the register batch case) and scripts/test-plan-refutation.mjs (the receipt cases). (2) Expected modes read context where they read review: scripts/test-outward-lint.mjs, scripts/test-target-publish.mjs and scripts/test-target-worktree-publish.mjs, whose marker loops also gain the context: marker. (3) The return of checkLocalTerms gains refuse, context and findings wherever a case compares it whole. (4) A mode word alone on a line no longer throws: the outward-lint list case asserts a section, and the malformed-list cases plant a line with no letter or digit ('refuse: ---'), whose message is 'no term on the line'. (5) The planning publish case no longer expects a refusal for a context-mode match in the body: the passing publish now lists that match and one in a line the branch adds. (6) Two cases plant a private term that runs across rows of the composed Change table ('0', then the next row's path). Runs on either side of a pipe are no longer one word, so the entries are spelled as the rows spell them, with the pipes between their runs ('0 | day', '0 | bridge.md | 1 | 0 | day'), which the entry's own characters join across; the mechanism those cases protect, a match's line range covering every contributing row, is unchanged and still exercised.",

    "git diff of the nine test and fixture files named above against the tree Part A began on",
    "node --test scripts/test-target-publish.mjs under the bounded wrapper at the first edit: 58 of 61 pass; the three failures were the mode word in two cases and the cross-row entry in one, each repaired as items (2) and (6) state",
    "node --test scripts/test-target-worktree-publish.mjs at the first edit: 20 of 23 pass; the three failures were the whole-value comparison of item (3), the mode word of item (2) and the cross-row entry of item (6)",
    "node --test scripts/test-vertical.mjs under the bounded wrapper: 165 pass with no edit"

```json

No word of the order changes: the lifecycle's joined text of all 133 criteria is identical before and after, so a criterion's hash is unchanged. At the base a wrapped line of that criterion began with <option>, which CommonMark reads as the start of an HTML block that runs to the next blank line; the list ended at criterion 78 and criteria 79 to 133 were one raw block. The lifecycle's line reader was unaffected and still read 133. The repair is made now because a rendered order showed 55 criteria as a block, and because Part B moves the criteria reader onto the parser, which would have read 78. At a worker's stop it held the parent's shell, the stopping worker itself as a subagent entry under its own agent id, and the worker's shell. An entry carries id, type, status and description, with command for a shell and agent_type for a subagent; the name field WO-139 recorded was not given. A listed task's id is the identifier its start returned: the Bash response's backgroundTaskId for a shell and the Agent response's agentId for a worker. A refused stop held the worker: it called TaskStop on its shell, and its stop re-entered with stop_hook_active true and the shell gone from the list. The parent was prompted after the worker's last stop, which is where its facts print. The hook therefore reads the list as the design item says of a session's list. It leaves out the entry whose id is the stopping worker's own agent id, since that entry is the worker and never a task it left running. It attributes each other live entry through the journal row the task's start wrote, keyed by a digest of that identifier and carrying the starter's digest where a worker's call started it. It counts as the worker's own only the tasks its calls started, refuses the stop once naming each by type and id with TaskStop as the tool that stops it, writes the stop to the parent session's journal under the worker's digest, and admits and records the re-entry. The parent's next facts name each worker whose last stop left a task of its own, or one no journaled call started, still running, until a later observation shows the task finished. (2) Every hour one Astra worker on Codex reads the execution as a critic of it: the approach of the code, the decisions, the order of the work, the gates run and the time. A critic's report is read the same way and answered in that decision: what is adopted and what is declined, with the reason. ## WO-276-D087 — Part M as built: a target order closes when its base holds the reviewed change by ancestry, a squash or a rebase, or under a commit named for it; the instance lists its authors; and the drive settles a target's own release

```json
{
  "id": "WO-276-D087",
  "date": "2026-11-12",
  "dispatch": "resume: next; WO-276 Part M (teams and merge methods), steps M1 to M4, its attack pass, rolling review 36 and the twenty-fourth critic, from 04:20 UTC",
  "decision": "Part M is built on checkpoint 40 (6538aaf0a, where D086 closed Part L) and its criteria 97 to 101 are judged in the handoff. Its two gates and its close are D088's. The merged check (step M1). scripts/lib/merged-change.mjs answers from Git alone whether a branch's change is in a fetched base: the branch is an ancestor of the base; or one commit of the base since the two diverged has the patch identity of the branch's whole change (a squash); or each of the branch's commits that is no merge has a commit of equal identity there (a rebase). It names the base commits matched and counts the base commits whose patches it read. Git's patch identity ignores whitespace and line numbers, as the git-patch-id manual of Git 2.31.0 says, and that release has no --verbatim, so an identity alone would take a change landed with other indentation, other line endings, a missing final newline or a path that differs by a space for the reviewed one, and the close would then delete the branch. Each identity match is therefore confirmed on the patch's own lines: every line as diff-tree prints it with full blob ids, without a hunk's position and, for a text file, without the blob ids a replayed patch legitimately changes; a binary file, which prints no content, is compared by its blobs. A merge of the branch that carries a change of its own (git diff-tree --cc prints something for it) is replayed by no commit, so a branch that holds one is not found as a rebase. A base that shares no history with the branch (rewritten since the branch was cut) matches nothing and no read fails. Where the base's patches are more than one read takes (256 MiB) the check says so and matches nothing. What is found for a pair of commits is kept for the process, so a close that asks at each of its sites reads the base's patches once. The named commit. Where the base holds the change under another patch nothing matches, and the close refuses with the source retained, the count of base commits read and the flag --merged-as <commit>. ## WO-276-D095 — The attack on the title rule: eight findings and a ninth the executor ran, repaired; the rule's boundary gains a second side, how often a body runs

```json
{
  "id": "WO-276-D095",
  "date": "2026-11-12",
  "dispatch": "resume: next; WO-276, during Part O: the part's attacker, given the title rule of criterion E1 as a second surface, from 09:12 UTC",
  "decision": "Part O's attacker (an Opus worker launched as the table's default, 09:12 to 09:18 UTC) was given two surfaces: the part's own change, on which it found nothing and which the part's as-built record reports, and the title rule as D094 left it, with the boundary that record wrote. It was asked for a suite file outside that boundary which the rule neither reports nor counts while node registers a title twice, or one the rule reports where node registers each title once. It returned eight, each run under node and against a standalone copy of the rule. The eight. (1) A title read from a name that is later given another value: the rule read the first value. (2) A registrar used as a template's tag: node registers a case under no name, and the rule read no call. (3) A registrar kept in a class's static field. (4) One taken by a destructuring assignment. (5) One taken by a logical assignment. (6) The module awaited by a specifier held in a name. (7) The module required through a function not named require. Each of (3) to (7) was neither reported nor counted, and each is a route that a declaration or an assignment of the file names, so D094's boundary was false of them. (8) A false report: the name test is read as a registrar whatever the file imports, and any member of a registrar as registering, so a file whose own variable or whose function's parameter is named test, with a method called on it, was reported for a title node registers once. It also judged the hooks: a hook's callback is handed a context through which cases register at the top level, which is a function's parameter and inside the boundary. A ninth, which the executor suspected while repairing and ran before believing: how often a body runs. A registration in a class's method, in an object's method, in a function kept in a property or in a list, and in a callback that one of the file's own functions calls twice is registered twice by node; the rule counted each once and none as unread. D094's boundary spoke only of how a registrar reaches a call. It had nothing to say of how often the call runs, and the rule counted any body it did not know as running once. The repairs. A title, and an import's specifier, is a fixed text only for a name bound once, to a literal, and never given another value by an assignment of any kind, an increment or a loop. A registrar used as a tag is a registration with a title the rule cannot read. A name is derived, and what is registered through it counted as unread, where a class declaration holds a registrar, where an assignment of any kind gives one to a name, to the names of a destructuring or to a member of an object (which derives the object, so a property written after its object was made is no longer silent), and where a loop runs over registrars. A module awaited by a specifier fixed in a name is read as that module, and the test module's name handed to any call makes the result a derived name. The name test is read as a registrar unless the file's top level declares it as a function or a class of its own or as a variable whose value holds no call; and a name that an enclosing function takes as a parameter, that a catch clause binds, or that a loop declares over something that is no registrar, is that binding. And a registration is counted exactly where the rule knows how often its body runs: at the top level, in one of the file's own named functions by the file's calls of it, in a function called where it is written, and in a class's static field or block; it is overstated on purpose in a loop and in a callback of a listed iteration, as before; and in any other body (a method, an accessor, a function kept in a property or a list, a callback handed to anything else, an instance field's value) it is counted as unread, as are the registrations of one of the file's own functions that is named other than to call it or is called from such a body. The boundary, as it now stands, has two sides. Unread, and never silent: a registrar reached through a derived name, by a computed key or by a callee that only names one; a tag; a title whose name has a second value or is built at run time; a registration in a body whose runs the rule cannot count. Silent: a registrar that reaches a call through a function's parameter or return value, a global, another module, or a module loaded by a specifier the file computes. The boundary files went from fourteen to thirty, twenty-six that the rule must count as unread and four on which it is silent, each run under node; the corpus gained four files, two of them controls for the false report; the family is unchanged at 335. One repair was wrong as first written and was caught by measurement. Finding (7) was first answered by treating any text that names the test module or the shard helper as a mention, anywhere in a value. Over the repository that made names derived from lists of paths, and five ordinary calls in two files were counted as unread registrations: the case's figure rose from 103 in 30 files to 108 in 31. Every suite file's unread count was then compared before and after the repairs, 177 files through a standalone copy of each version of the rule; the two files and the five calls were named, and the rule narrowed to a module imported or required in place and to the test module's name handed to a call. No file's count now differs, and the figure is again 103 in 30. The first recheck (the same worker re-tasked, 09:29 to 09:32 UTC) found all eight holding as repaired and five more, each run and all of one cause: the rule kept its tables by a name's spelling. A title's name that a function declaration shadows where it is used was read as the outer text, and a var read before its declaration as its initializer, both in silence. A local variable named test in a function or a block was taken for the registrar, and a local function or a parameter with a helper's name inflated that helper's count, each into a report of a repeat node does not register. And an unrelated binding or a method with a helper's name made the helper's once-only registrations unread. The shadowing and seed rules written at 09:19 for finding (8) were two more approximations by name, and three of the five came out of them within the quarter hour. The repair is one change. fileBindings resolves every name to the declaration it stands for by the scopes the language gives (a module's imports and declarations, a function's parameters, its body's var declarations, a block's let, const, class and function declarations, a loop's own declarations, a catch clause's variable, an expression's own name), key gives one text for each declaration, and the forty-one lookups and writes that went by a name's text go by that key; a name that is no use of a variable, a member's name, a property's key or a method's name, matches nothing. The shadowing rule is deleted. A fixed text is that of a const or let binding alone. The second recheck (09:39 to 09:41 UTC) found the five holding and five more in the resolver and around it. A parameter's default value was resolved into the body's var declarations, which is a scope apart in the language: a registrar named there was missed in silence. A var declared again kept its first value's reading, and the name test was read as a registrar when imported from any module or taken at the top level out of any call's result: three false reports. And a typed file's namespace that holds a registrar was no holder the rule knew. The resuming session compared the working tree with that checkpoint through an index file in scratch before any edit: no path differed and none was untracked. What the part builds, as the order's design decides it and this record is linked for. The bound measures work. A phase's wall-clock value is the time since its dispatch began less every idle gap, and a gap is idle only when three things hold: it begins at a turn's end row of one of the phase's sessions (a row whose event is Stop), it is longer than the idle interval (ten minutes, the planner's first figure, a named constant beside the reading), and no tool call's start row and end row lie on either side of it. A tool call is paired by session and tool: an end row belongs to the earliest start row of that tool the session has open, so the time between them is worked however long it is, and a worker's call that is still running when the root's turn ends keeps that wait worked. Everything else counts as worked: the time before the first row, a long turn whose rows are far apart, a session that crashed without an end row. Where no session of the phase wrote a turn's end row the value is the elapsed time, as before this part. The standing keeps the elapsed time since the dispatch as a field of its own and prints it beside the value when the two differ. The phase's sessions are the ones whose journals hold the same dispatch anchor (role, dispatch line, order and start); the rows of all of them are read together, so one session's stop while another works is no gap. A dispatch that names no order starts at its own session (step P6): the hook's binding takes an earlier start only from the session's own earlier binding, and the anchor reader returns none for it, so a planning pass inherits neither an earlier pass's start nor its complete runs. An executor redispatched in the same phase of one order keeps the earliest start, as before. The figure is the instance's and advisory. spend.daily in the budgets file holds tokens, usd or both, each a positive number or null. The prompt hook reads the budgets file's own key first and reads the usage ledger only where a figure is declared; the day's use is the usage report's own reading (the ledger's rows by local calendar day, each observation counted for what it adds), so the line and npm run meta -- --usage agree. At or above the figure the line says to finish the step in hand, write the standing and end the turn. A dollar figure whose day holds a session with no declared price, or one that attests no model, prints the day's tokens and unknown for the estimate. Nothing is refused. The standing is docs/evidence/WO-NNN/standing.md, written by the executor at a stop and replaced at the next: the steps done, the step in hand and its state, what comes next, what is undecided. ## WO-276-D131 — The repair of VER-002: ten findings in code, each closed as the class it names

```json
{
  "id": "WO-276-D131",
  "date": "2026-11-13",
  "dispatch": "resume: fix; repair of VER-002, its ten blocking findings in code (F1, F2, F4, F5, F7 to F11 and F18)",
  "decision": "Each finding is repaired as the class it names, with the rule the repaired code holds and cases the report did not quote. F6, the missing reader comparisons, is evidence and is WO-276-D132's. F1 (criterion 18). Cause: the pattern-reader screen chose its sources by a suffix list of its own, .mjs under scripts/ and .ts, .mts, .mjs and .js under a package's src/, narrower than the dialects the source reader parses. Rule: the screen selects every non-test source under both roots whose suffix the source reader's dialect rule admits (a module, a CommonJS file or a plain file, of JavaScript or TypeScript, with JSX or not), and a path handed to it that the reader parses in no dialect is refused by name, never counted as a source that passed. Cases: a checkout with a pattern reader in each of the twelve suffixes under scripts/, a nested scripts directory and a package's src/ (thirty-six files, each refused by file and line); the same suffixes as a suite, a named test, a fixture and a package test, and four files that are no source, none selected; the selection and the reader agreeing on every selected path; the refusal of an unparsed path. F2 (criterion 103). Cause: under records kept in the instance, the target publish compared the paths a reviewed change touched with the order's record paths, so a deletion counted as holding a record. Rule: the reviewed tree is judged; a touched record path is held only where the reviewed commit's tree holds a file at it. An added or edited record is still refused by name, an untouched one the base held is left alone, and a removed one files nothing. Cases: a change that removes two earlier-cycle records beside a product file publishes at the reviewed commit; a change that removes one such record and edits another is refused naming the edited one alone, with nothing pushed. F4 (criterion 17). Cause: the working-tree snapshot staged the tree into an empty temporary index, where an ignore rule also hides a tracked file. Rule: the snapshot holds every file Git tracks as the working tree holds it, and every untracked file no ignore rule matches. It still stages from an empty index, so every file is read from the working tree whatever the real index says of it; it then adds, by name, each file the real index tracks that the first pass left out and the working tree still holds, which no ignore rule judges. A tracked file the tree lost stays out, and the real index is untouched. The first form of this repair copied the real index instead, and the combined review showed that the copy carries Git's assume-unchanged and skip-worktree flags, under which a changed file was captured as committed where main captured its change (WO-276-D133). The target draft's own snapshot, which started from HEAD and so dropped a file added to the index by force and not yet committed, now calls the same function. Cases, in the checkpoint case of the resume suite: a tracked file changed and then matched by a new rule; a file added by force under a rule and never committed; an ignored untracked file; a file staged and then removed; a file Git is told to assume unchanged and one it is told to skip, each changed afterwards; the index compared before and after. F5 (criterion 21). Cause: the header reader cut the document at the first line that looked like the header's end and parsed the text before it, so whatever that line stood in (a code span opened above it, a link, a quotation's lazy line) was decided by the cut and not by the parser. Rule: the header read from an order's lead is the header the whole document gives. The cut is made after the first blank line that follows the candidate line, so the parser reads the candidate and its whole paragraph, and the lead's reading stands only where the parser itself finds the header's end in it; otherwise the whole document is parsed. Two things the lead cannot show are read from the text and answered with the whole document: a document that opens with a front-matter delimiter (front matter is front matter only where its closer follows), and a closing bracket with a colon below the cut (a link or footnote definition there makes a bracketed label above it a reference, which can take a line's bold label inside a link; observed with the pinned parser). A block left open at the cut runs to the end of the text the parser was handed (a fence, a comment or another HTML block, a math block; each observed), so a candidate inside one is no end to the parser either. Cases: thirty-two documents compared field for field with the whole-document reading, among them the report's two, emphasis, a link's text, inline HTML, a comment in a paragraph, inline math, lazy lines of a quotation and a list item, five kinds of open block, both kinds of front matter, three references whose definitions stand in the body, five ends of the header the line scan does not see, carriage returns and a byte-order mark; each also asserts whether the lead alone was parsed. Over the 269 committed orders the two readers agree on every field, 268 are read from the lead alone, and the header reading takes 580 ms where whole documents take 2,056 ms (516 ms before the repair, measured the same way in session scratch). F7 (criterion 101). Cause: the drive's route read a close record's own attempt and the eight before it, while the close itself also reads the archives the record names. Rule: the route reads the same history as the close, through one reader (scripts/lib/close-history.mjs, which writes nothing): the record, its eight, its retained attempt and every attempt its archives hold, each still held to the order, to a real attempt and to the current activation. An archive that cannot be read gives nothing, so the order routes to the close, which names it. Cases: a settled close followed by twelve attempts, dry runs and publishes stopped in their prerequisites by turns, released at each; the same history after a reactivation, not released; an archive whose bytes changed, not released and named by the close; an archive name outside the order's history, not followed. F8 (criterion 64). Cause: the host report read which hosts the instance has on inside an attempt whose failure it then ignored, and read a tool's version through a reader that answered every failure as an absent tool. Rule: a fact the report cannot read is reported as not read and changes no exit code. Where the elections cannot be read it says so in a row marked unknown and looks for no elected host's CLI. A tool that is on the path and does not answer for its version is reported found and unread: that leaves the forge row unknown where nothing else of it is unmet, and an agent CLI's row, which is never judged, says the same. The tool reads were the combined review's finding, of the class this one names (WO-276-D133). Cases: the elections readable with a host on; unreadable with every other fact met (one unknown row, ten rows, exit 0, Claude Code's CLI still looked for, no elected host's asked); unreadable beside a Node below the floor (exit 1, by the floor); gh not answering (the forge row unknown, exit 0); gh absent (unmet, exit 1); gh not answering beside an origin the helpers refuse (unmet); an agent CLI not answering. F9 (criterion 65). Cause: the report's sanitizer bounded a path's segment and an address's parts by ASCII word characters. Rule: a segment and an address part are whatever is not white space, in any script; a slash opens an absolute path where no letter or digit of any script, underscore, period, hyphen or opening angle bracket stands before it, so the report's own words with a slash stand. Cases: eight values on the injected Node version, among them paths in Latin with diacritics, Han and Cyrillic, a quoted path, an scp-style address, a share, a drive path and a URL with a non-ASCII host; each printed row keeps the words around the value. A path with a space in a name is withheld up to the space, which no pattern can bound; the kit guide states that limit and the reopening condition names it. F10 (regression against main). Cause: the admission of an appended execution record refused every bold field the Markdown reader finds after the approved bytes, in any container. Rule: an appended record may hold no label of the order's own, by the work-order reader's own distinction: a bold phrase that opens a line of a top-level paragraph and declares a value by its colon or stands alone on its line. What the reader takes for text is admitted: a label in a list item, a quotation or a code block, and bold words that open a line and run on into their sentence. The first form of this repair refused every bold phrase that opens a top-level line, and the combined review showed that it refused plain emphasis main admitted (WO-276-D133). Cases, through the plan gate: four more refusals (an own field after a list, one that continues a paragraph, a section label alone on its line, a label in lower case) and eleven admissions (bulleted and numbered items, a quotation, a quotation inside an item, a fenced example, bold words in the middle of a line, and five lines that open with emphasis: a digit first, a code span first, after another line of the paragraph, a capital first, lower case). Against main: a fenced example and a line that opens with capitalized emphasis are admitted where main's line pattern refused them, and a label in lower case is refused where main admitted it, since the reader takes it for the order's metadata (the verifier's briefing reads the Known issues label in any case). F11 (criterion 115). Cause: the day's least amounts were rebuilt from group aggregates, and a group's estimate and total are null where any of its observations has none. Rule: the usage reading carries, beside each whole figure, what a group is known to have used at the least (knownTokens, knownUsd), summed an observation at a time: an observation's total where its host reported one and the classes it reported where it did not, and its estimate where it has one. The day's line reads those. Cases, each through the prompt's renderer: a measured session beside an uncounted one of the same role, of another role, of another order and one that attests no model (least amounts unchanged, the figure reached at $50 and at the token total, not at $61); a later uncounted observation of the measured session (figures whole); a host that reports a total and no cache split, alone and beside an uncounted session (the total, never the one class); a total and a class sum added together. F18 (criterion 127). Cause: a withdrawal that is an order's first event recorded the order's file and not the registered repository the file declares, which only an activation bound; the index compares the two for every order the log knows. Rule: the withdrawal of a never-activated order records the repository identity its file declares, id and base commit, as filed and registered still or not, and the fold binds it under the check an activation's identity passes. Cases: the real command withdraws a launchpad order and a target order that were never activated, the index lists both as withdrawn and its check passes; a file whose declaration then moves is refused as an activated order's is; a first-event withdrawal without the identity, with half of one, with the reserved id or with no commit id is refused by name. Met and not changed: the host report's fallback row, printed when its library cannot load, prints Node's version as given; that value is process.version, which holds no path, so no writer produces the input and no code changed. The failure census of close records (scripts/lib/plan-failures.mjs) reads a record's own attempts by design, as product 07 states, and judges no completion. VER-002's follow-up row, FUP-c5343087653dc9a9, names these repairs and seven planning items; the repairs are done here and the planning items (F3 and F12 to F17) are carried by this decision's follow-up.",

## WO-276-D183 — The ladder's second round: two regressions the first round's repairs left or made, each closed as its class, and five lesser findings

Each brief added the section on the failed report the first round's carried and the complete return contract, the schema itself (WO-276-D182); all three returned a report the recorder accepted with no re-task. Fresh workers, not continuations of the first round's, since a recheck brief asks for the whole change to be judged again and a review is not continued into a second judgment. Rechecks: criteria.1.F1 and design.1.F1 not held; criteria.1.F2 to F6, design.1.F2 to F7 and consistency.1.F1 and F2 held. Eight findings, seven distinct, this decision's reviewFindings, each judged with the rule the repaired code now holds. Class criterion, fixed. (1) criteria.2.F1, the class of criteria.1.F1 still open. The first round's closing check read the node that ends the criteria block and the one node after it. A wrapped line that opens with a number sign and is followed by one more wrapped line makes a heading and then a paragraph that holds the later items, and a note between the closing heading or label and the items that go on hides them as well: every reader returned the shorter list where main read all. The check now reads everything the closing label or heading leads, to the next label or heading: a line inside any block there from which the numbering resumes at the next criterion, or the first ordered list there starting at it, is refused. The resumption test parses only from a line that opens like an item of the number sought, so its cost stays with the lines that could resume; that line test is the shared module's (orderedListStart in markdown-links.mjs), since the document check's Markdown screen refused it written in the criteria reader as a second grammar of the list. The case holds the reviewer's four shapes. (2) design.2.F1 and consistency.2.F1, a link whose text opens with a bracketed word. WO-276-D178's neutral copy replaced the first bracket of every pair of opening brackets, so that no wiki link could form; a bracket means something to CommonMark, so a link written `[[DRAFT] the plan](missing-plan.md)` was no link and the link check passed its missing target, where main failed it. The copy now takes a wiki link apart only where the extension would read one, by the carried parser's own rule: two opening brackets, a target on one line holding no closing bracket and a character that is not a space or a tab, and two closing brackets, with no alias divider, which Prettier's configuration never matches. There the inner bracket of each pair is replaced, and the outer two keep the meaning CommonMark gives them, so a link whose text opens with a bracketed word, or whose text is one (`[[draft]](url)`, which the extension read as a wiki link on main and in the first round, and which main's pattern-based product links read), is read as written; a wiki link alone stays text. The cases hold the link and image shapes the reviewers wrote, a wiki link that stays text, and the link check over a page holding a missing target in each shape. Class lesser, fixed. (3) design.2.F2: a source that already held one of the three private-use characters was parsed as written, so a link between two dollar figures went unseen there. The copy's characters are now chosen for each source from the private-use range, four the source does not hold; only a source holding all 6,400 is parsed as written. (4) design.2.F3: a label or a heading the author set at the margin between groups of criteria was refused with the remedy for a wrapped line. The refusal now tells the two apart by the closing line: indented, or written straight after a line of the list, it is a wrapped line of an item; at the margin after a blank line, it sets a group, and the remedy is to name the group in its items' text, such as (B1), as this order's own criteria do.
